era.title: The Natural History Museum Opens, 1881
era.summary: On 18 April 1881 the British Museum (Natural History) opened free to all in South Kensington, in a Romanesque building designed by Alfred Waterhouse. The Times called it a 'true Temple of Nature,' though The Field thought it more suited to a suburban tea-garden. Richard Owen, the first superintendent, wanted a 'cathedral to nature' anyone could visit free of charge. The record for local dress, street lighting and traffic in 1881 is thin, so those details are not filled in here.
funFacts: The museum opened on 18 April 1881 as the British Museum (Natural History); it was not formally renamed the Natural History Museum until 1992.
Alfred Waterhouse designed the building in a Romanesque style with an iron frame and brick and terracotta walls; the terracotta came from Gibbs and Canning of Tamworth.
The revised tender was £352,000, and the contractors failed in the summer of 1879 while the museum was nearly finished.
The site was the former site of the 1862 International Exhibition, demolished after Parliament vetoed the purchase of the exhibition building in July 1863.
Richard Owen, the first superintendent, wanted a 'cathedral to nature' that anyone could visit free of charge.
The transfer of collections from Bloomsbury was not fully complete until 1883.

sceneBrief.description: Facing north from Cromwell Road, about 45 metres south of the museum, the view is filled by the newly opened Waterhouse façade: a long, symmetrical terracotta front with a central gable and twin towers, set back behind a forecourt with iron railings and a gate lodge. The building is complete externally and open, but the gardens are still incomplete, with only the path layout achieved and limited planting. The central gable is surmounted by a single figure of Adam.

persists: The Waterhouse front, front lodge, gates and railings still survive.
altered: The setting is now a busy arterial road and the museum is surrounded by much later buildings.
notYetBuilt: The former Geology Museum/Earth Galleries of 1929–33.
The pedestrian subway under Exhibition Road, largely completed in 1885.
gone: The 1862 International Exhibition building, already demolished after the 1863 veto.

sceneBrief.surroundings: North: the museum itself fills the immediate view; beyond it, the central axis of the building is aligned with the Royal Albert Hall and the Albert Memorial further north. East: the South Kensington Museum — now the Victoria and Albert Museum — lies east along Cromwell Road/Exhibition Road. South: Cromwell Road and the residential terraces and stucco houses of the newly developed South Kensington estate. West: Gloucester Road, its station and the surrounding residential streets and mews. Immediate foreground: the museum forecourt, railings and gate lodge.

guide.name: Thomas Carter
guide.bio: I'm a porter here at the new museum, and I've been with the building since the last of the scaffolding came down. I show visitors to the doors and keep an eye on the railings and the forecourt.
guide.appearance: A man of about 50, stout and sturdy, wearing a dark blue porter's coat with brass buttons, a peaked cap, and a white shirt with a dark necktie.
guide.script: Hello there, I'm Thomas Carter, one of the porters here. You've come on a fine day to see our new museum, opened on the eighteenth of April, 1881. Mr Waterhouse designed it in the Romanesque style, with brick and terracotta walls — the terracotta came from Gibbs and Canning of Tamworth. The tenders came to three hundred and fifty-two thousand pounds, and the contractors failed in the summer of seventy-nine, just as we were nearly finished. Mr Owen, our first superintendent, wanted a cathedral to nature that anyone could visit free of charge, and free it is. Mind the path as you go — the gardens aren't finished yet. Good day to you.
guide.greeting: Good morning, sir or madam. I'm Thomas Carter, the porter here — welcome to the new museum. Mind your step on the forecourt; the gardens aren't quite finished yet.
